abstract: Precise control of nanoscale architectures makes DNA origami a promising platform for biomedical applications such as drug delivery, biosensing, and bioimaging. A key constraint in DNA origami design is that crossover placement must account for the helical pitch of DNA. For new learners, however, it can be difficult to understand how a DNA helical pitch affects assembled structures. Here, we report a hands-on laboratory module to teach undergraduate students about this fundamental helical pitch/structure relationship. A rectangular DNA origami tile is designed as a model system with its helical pitch varying from 10.5 to 10.84 base-pairs per turn. When the tiles are linked into a ribbon, the small mismatch-driven deformations of individual tiles accumulate into a global twist. The twist appears as characteristic kinks under atomic force microscopy (AFM). In a five-day pilot, three engineering students designed the DNA origami tile and used CanDo finite-element simulations to predict its deformations at different helical pitches. They assembled ribbons and used an intercalator, ethidium bromide (EtBr), to vary DNA helicity without changing the crossover layout. With increasing EtBr concentration, all three participants observed the ribbon chirality transition from right-handed to flat to left-handed conformations. By comparing predictions with their own observations, students gain a practical understanding of how DNA helicity governs DNA structure design.
